evidence.claim: early roadside parks

evidence.claim: a courthouse won by votes
evidence.quote: The vote was held in 1888 to decide the location of the county seat; Crystal Falls won by only 5 votes.

evidence.claim: Between Iron River and Crystal Falls, US 2 runs east through forest near small lakes, ending this drive beside a courthouse on a hilltop.
evidence.quote: US 2 leaves the Ottawa National Forest at Iron River, and the highway continues eastward through forest lands near several small lakes to Crystal Falls, the county seat of Iron County.

evidence.claim: ending this drive beside a courthouse on a hilltop.
evidence.quote: next to the county courthouse at the top of the hill.

evidence.claim: This section is the Iron County Heritage Trail, a Pure Michigan Byway designated to honor mining and logging.
evidence.quote: The section of US 2 between Iron River and Crystal Falls has been named the Iron County Heritage Trail. This Pure Michigan Byway was designated to honor the "rich history of two industries that built a state and nation: mining and logging."

evidence.claim: Crystal Falls developed as a center of iron mining and the timber industry.
evidence.quote: The area first developed as a major center for iron mining and the timber industry

evidence.claim: The road’s numbering changed before its modern route settled: M-12 was in use by 1919, and US 2 replaced part of it in 1926.
evidence.quote: The first state trunkline highway designated along the path of the modern US 2 was M‑12, a designation that was in use by July 1, 1919

evidence.claim: US 2 replaced part of it in 1926.
evidence.quote: When the US Highway System was created on November 11, 1926, US 2 partially replaced M-12.

evidence.claim: Near Iron River, Herbert Larson created an early roadside park in 1919–20.
evidence.quote: The first roadside park in the country was created by Herbert Larson near what is now US 2 near Iron River in 1919–20.

evidence.claim: As engineer-manager of the county road commission, he bought land and wide road rights of way for public parks, seeking surviving stands of virgin timber.
evidence.quote: Larson purchased for the county individual tracts of land as well as wide rights of way along what is now US-2, to be set aside as parks for public use. He particularly looked for and obtained some of the last stands of virgin timber in the county.

evidence.claim: As engineer-manager of the county road commission
evidence.quote: Herbert F. Larson was appointed as engineer-manager of the Iron County Road Commission in 1917.

evidence.claim: In Iron River, the highway shifted again in 1998, leaving its former bridge on Genesee Street to carry local traffic. The road’s history is visible in that bypassed crossing as well as in the parks developed along its route.
evidence.quote: In 1998, US-2 was relocated, and the section where this bridge stands left to carry local traffic.

evidence.claim: its former bridge on Genesee Street
evidence.quote: is a bridge located on Genesee Street (a bypassed segment of U.S. Route 2) over the Iron River

evidence.claim: Start in Iron River, which absorbed Stambaugh and Mineral Hills in 2000.
evidence.quote: On November 2, 1999, the voters of the cities of Iron River and Stambaugh and the village of Mineral Hills approved consolidation into a new city, which continued the name Iron River. The consolidation became effective July 1, 2000.

evidence.claim: East along US 2, Bewabic State Park occupies the shore of Fortune Lake west of Crystal Falls.
evidence.quote: Bewabic State Park is a public recreation area covering 315 acres (127 ha) on the shore of Fortune Lake (First Lake), four miles (6.4 km) west of Crystal Falls

evidence.claim: East along US 2, Bewabic State Park
evidence.quote: on the bank of Fortune Lake and the south side of US 2.

evidence.claim: At Crystal Falls, US 2 joins US 141 on Crystal Avenue, then turns onto 5th Street to meet M-69 beside the county courthouse.
evidence.quote: On the west side of town, US 2 meets US 141; the two highways run concurrently along Crystal Avenue. The combined highway turns south onto 5th Street and meets M‑69's eastern terminus at the intersection between 5th Street and Superior Avenue next to the county courthouse at the top of the hill.

evidence.claim: Stambaugh’s name came from a mine owner: John Stambaugh, president of Todd, Stambaugh Co., had recently bought the Iron River Mine when the town was platted in 1882.
evidence.quote: The settlemented was platted in 1882 and named for John Stambaugh, president of the Todd, Stambaugh Co., who had recently purchased the Iron River Mine, which was located at the townsite.

evidence.claim: The mine occupied the townsite.
evidence.quote: the Iron River Mine, which was located at the townsite.

evidence.claim: Stambaugh later became a city in 1923.
evidence.quote: The village incorporated as a city in 1923.

evidence.claim: Voters approved consolidation with Iron River and Mineral Hills in 1999, and the combined city took the Iron River name on July 1, 2000.
evidence.quote: On November 2, 1999, the voters of the cities of Iron River and Stambaugh and the village of Mineral Hills approved consolidation into a new city, which continued the name Iron River. The consolidation became effective July 1, 2000.

evidence.claim: Herbert Larson created a roadside park near Iron River in 1919–20.
evidence.quote: The first roadside park in the country was created by Herbert Larson near what is now US 2 near Iron River in 1919–20.

evidence.claim: His work extended beyond roadbuilding: as engineer-manager of the Iron County Road Commission, he acquired land along what is now US 2 for public parks.
evidence.quote: Larson purchased for the county individual tracts of land as well as wide rights of way along what is now US-2, to be set aside as parks for public use.

evidence.claim: as engineer-manager of the Iron County Road Commission
evidence.quote: Herbert F. Larson was appointed as engineer-manager of the Iron County Road Commission in 1917.

evidence.claim: He sought some of the county’s remaining stands of virgin timber.
evidence.quote: He particularly looked for and obtained some of the last stands of virgin timber in the county.

evidence.claim: A fieldstone wall built in 1936 lines US 2 at Bewabic State Park.
evidence.quote: A cut fieldstone wall, constructed by the CCC in 1936, lines US 2.

evidence.claim: The park began with Herbert Larson’s purchase of a Fortune Lake farmstead in 1923, including a stand of virgin timber.
evidence.quote: Bewabic Park was created in 1923, when Larson purchased a 120-acre farmstead on Fortune Lake containing a stand of virgin timber.

evidence.claim: Civil Works Administration crews improved it in 1933; Civilian Conservation Corps workers followed from 1935 to 1937.
evidence.quote: One hundred and seventy CWA workers were assigned to Bewabic Park in 1933.

evidence.claim: Civilian Conservation Corps workers followed from 1935 to 1937.
evidence.quote: In 1935, one hundred and eight CCC workers began work in Bewabic Park, and continued until 1937.

evidence.claim: Their surviving work includes the wall and a log bathhouse above the lake.
evidence.quote: A log bathhouse constructed by the CCC in 1937 sits at the top of the hill above the lake.

evidence.claim: The island reached by a footbridge was once a peninsula: workers dug a separating canal in 1933.
evidence.quote: Originally a peninsula, the island was created in 1933 by CWA workers who dug a canal to separate it from the main shore. A short wood plank footbridge crosses the canal

evidence.claim: Michigan purchased the park in 1966, making the former county recreation ground part of its state park system.
evidence.quote: In 1966, Bewabic Park was purchased by the state of Michigan as part of an acquisition program to substantially expand the state park system.

evidence.claim: Law, Mercy and Justice stand above the courthouse entrance as 17-foot zinc statues.
evidence.quote: Above the archway are the impressive 17-feet-high zinc statues representing Law, Mercy, and Justice.

evidence.claim: They were added in 1910 to a building whose location had provoked a county-wide dispute.
evidence.quote: The clocktower and statutes representing Law, Mercy, and Justice were added in 1910.

evidence.claim: Iron River became county seat when Iron County formed in 1885, but men from Crystal Falls carried off its county records.
evidence.quote: At one point county records were spirited away from the temporary courthouse in Iron River by men from Crystal Falls.

evidence.claim: Iron River became county seat when Iron County formed in 1885
evidence.quote: Iron County was established in 1885, when it was split from Marquette County.  At the time of Iron County's creation, Iron River, then the only incorporated village in the county, was designated the county seat.

evidence.claim: Crystal Falls won the 1888 referendum by five votes, then won again in 1889 by nearly 100.
evidence.quote: Crystal Falls won by only 5 votes.  In 1889, the question was again put before voters, and this time Crystal Falls was selected by a margin of nearly 100 votes

evidence.claim: The resulting courthouse has reddish-brown brick walls and stone trim, overlooking the town’s business street.
evidence.quote: The Iron County Courthouse is a 2+1⁄2-story Richardsonian Romanesque building sitting on a hilltop overlooking Crystal Falls' business street. It is built with reddish brown brick walls with stone trim

evidence.claim: Architect J. C. Clancy of Antigo, Wisconsin, designed the building after bonds were issued to fund construction.
evidence.quote: Bonds were issued for $30,000 to fund courthouse construction, and architect J. C. Clancy of Antigo, Wisconsin was engaged to design the courthouse.

evidence.claim: Three zinc figures stand above the granite entrance arch: Law, Mercy and Justice.
evidence.quote: Above the archway are the impressive 17-feet-high zinc statues representing Law, Mercy, and Justice.

evidence.claim: granite entrance arch
evidence.quote: A rock-face granite central archway contains the main entrance
